reviews.title: AI Disinformation strikes again
reviews.text: I was hoping to cut down on distracting app use by learning new things, but there’s nothing to learn from AI-generated writing besides the fact that you can’t trust anything as a source of information anymore. The devs claim everything is human-reviewed before publishing, but I’ve seen a few too many lessons with the text stumbling over itself to poorly explain the topic, quiz questions with completely nonsensical explanations, and source links where the supposed information is nowhere to be found. The multiple reviews about finding lessons that are entirely false only confirms this app to be full of AI hallucinations. It’s malice to promote AI writing as educational, corrupt to profit off spreading disinformation (that you didn’t even write!), and just humiliating to rely on this proven BS in the age of information.

reviews.title: Great concept, but it hallucinates a lot
reviews.text:
As the title says, I really like this app. It’s a great idea, easy to use, and I’ve learned some interesting stuff from it. However, once I had been using it for a few weeks, I noticed a troubling pattern: it was hallucinating entire topics and occasionally giving me lessons that were utterly incoherent. For some reason, this seems to be a particularly heinous problem in the “Crime” category. 

Weird prompts I’ve been given include “The Murder of Steve Irwin,” “The Murder of John McCain,” and perhaps most jarringly of all, “The Guilty Conscience of Ad**f H**ler.” Whenever these prompts come up for me, the text of the lesson inevitably devolves into the app arguing with itself, saying things like “there is no evidence that this actually happened” or “present lesson to user in conversational, educational tone.” In each case, it clarified that Steve Irwin and John McCain, respectively, were not murdered; it also clarified that there’s no evidence H**ler felt any remorse.

The most baffling one was when I got a lesson called “The Kidnapping of Edna K,” in which the app immediately acknowledged it had no idea of such an event ever occurring. It proceeded to create a five page lesson listing various criminal cases from various countries that could be related, before repeatedly determining that there was no “kidnapping of Edna K” that it could identify. 

A very user friendly app and great concept, but the content needs a lot of work. When the entire purpose of your product is to share knowledge, fake AI hallucinations are just about the worst thing you could have happen.

reviews.title: Another Cool Premise Ruined By AI…
reviews.text:
I love fun facts and learning new trivia, so I was initially very excited about this app. Although, I did find it was sometimes difficult to come across topics that I didn’t already know about. Which I assume would be an issue for anyone that’s a trivia buff, as well. 

I also found that the AI generator used had a difficult time articulating certain topics. I have an interest in philosophy and could not find a single prompt that explained in detail any school of thought, it would read more as “this thing exists,” which is pretty obvious. But I wanted to know WHY it exists, how it influences things, an explanation on WHAT it is, even.

The absolute worst AI offenses were in the crime category, though. Several times the prompt title would reference a crime or case and the year it occurred. Then upon starting the lesson, you’d read (apparently no more than 350 words) about how no results could be found for that prompt, thus it didn’t exist—completely wasting one of your three lessons allowed each day if you’re freemium.
The worst lesson I’ve read, I just experienced; It was an AI generated prompt that detailed returns on crimes against a family of four in the 90’s. There were apparently about 12 results found, and then you read through how it “reasoned” which crime it should expand upon, how it excluded certain crimes (“not in the 90’s”, or “victims not a family of four”,) and that it should all be summarized within 350 words.

I’ll be deleting the app. I don’t want to read AI slop scraped from the internet that clearly isn’t verified or reviewed by a human being for accuracy. And I find it especially atrocious that the developer thinks you should pay for an app when they use AI to churn out “lessons” that may or may not be factual.

reviews.title: Bad quizzes + weak lessons
reviews.text:
Many quiz questions are wrong. For example, one quiz question asks which topic wasn’t mentioned in the article, and all choices were mentioned so the question had no correct answer. The app says the right answer is radio telescopes, but that topic is clearly mentioned in the article. This is just one example, but I noticed that over 70% of the quiz questions have some mistake in them. 

And the articles all seem to be AI generated. I don’t know for sure but it seems obvious from the way the articles are written. But with better prompts I can generate better articles myself. It would be nicer if the articles had some human touch to them. 

I gave it more than 1 star because the app seems to be very well designed with a very good UI. But the content itself is weak (I picked the 5 minute lessons which have the longest articles)

reviews.title: Hate the changes
reviews.text:
I've had this app for a year now, I got it as soon as it came out. I really enjoyed swiping through the cards and learning new things at my leisure. I would save the best ones and read them with my husband before bed. 
I just got on the app after a few months of not using it as I've been really busy, and the entire app has changed. 

Now you only get so many topics and the rest seem to be locked until you finish whatever lesson unlocks it, but it doesn't say which one. So I can no longer just pick up the app in my downtime and learn. 

I'm forced into a gamified system that I DON'T want. Isn't the point for people to learn about what they find interesting? Way to completely ruin it. Deleted the app.
